newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia retail sales still soft.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia retail sales still soft.

text.p: Australian retail trade data for December are expected to show a rise for the third consecutive month but are also seen confirming the flat state of the ecomomy by showing a fall in real terms in the fourth quarter.
The figures are due at 0030 GMT (11.30 a.m.) on Tuesday.

Three interest rate cuts in the second half of 1996 are yet to show much impact on consumer spending and a weak December result on the day the Reserve Bank holds its first board meeting fore the year would heighten market expectations of a fourth.
On the monthly data, the median forecast of the 29 economists surveyed by Reuters was for a 0.5 percent rise. Forecasts ranged from a 1.0 percent fall to a 1.5 percent rise.
Anecdotal evidence suggests retailers did not have a very happy Christmas and several announced profit downgrades on the back of disappointing Christmas sales.
However, economists generally said December retail trade was still expected to have been postive.
"Despite a spattering of anecdotal reports to the contrary, on the whole retailing is expected to have exerienced positive conditions over the month," Dresdner chief economist Rob Henderson said.
Economists said that much of the pessimism, and downgrades, were associated with the clothing sector, but other sectors, such as food and recreational goods, had held up fairly well.
If retail trade does rise in December, it will be the third consecutive rise in the monthly series.
Despite this, retail trade will still have not recovered all the ground lost in September's 3.7 percent fall.

This means that once the nominal figures are adjusted to constant price terms using a retail price deflator, fourth quarter real retail trade is expected to have posted a fall in the quarter, in turn implying a detraction from fourth quarter gross domestic product (GDP).
The median forecast of economists was for a 0.5 percent fall in quarterly retail trade. Forecasts for the quarterly data range from a fall of 1.1 percent to a flat result.

Commonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney said the anecdotal reports on Christmas spending were mixed, although fundamentals would suggest that recent employment strength -- employment rose by almost 55,000 in the fourth quarter -- combined with the three rate cuts since July should have boosted activity.
"However, our own data suggests that spending was relatively weak in the December quarter," he said, forecasting a 0.9 percent fall in real trade over the quarter.

Retail trade accounts for about one quarter of GDP, and while a negative quarterly result does not mean GDP will be negative, as one of the first partial GDP indicators a weak figure could impact on sentiment on the chances of a rate cut.
"Weak retail spending implies a soft December quarter GDP," Colonial State Bank chief economist Has Kunnen said.
